narrationScript: While explicitly calling `close()` is vital, Python offers a much safer and more convenient way to handle files: the `with` statement. This is the preferred method because it acts as a context manager, automatically handling the opening and, crucially, the closing of the file for you, even if errors occur within the block. This prevents resource leaks and simplifies your code. Once a file is open, you'll want to read its contents. The `file.read()` method reads the entire file into a single string. Be mindful with very large files, as this can consume a lot of memory. If you need to process data line by line, `file.readline()` reads just one line at a time, including the newline character. And if you want all lines as a list of strings, `file.readlines()` will do the trick. However, for memory efficiency, especially with large files, iterating directly over the file object with a `for` loop is often the best approach. Each iteration yields one line, and you can use `line.strip()` to remove leading or trailing whitespace, including the newline character, for cleaner processing.
